title: The Trinity Speaks in Us, Gives Us Life, Law and Name
english: That the Trinity speaks in the faithful because its nature and essence admit no variation.

The divine hypostases speak alike in the saints, and this too proclaims that their nature and authority admit no variation. For Zechariah, not the prophet but the father of John, said that the Lord, the God of Israel, had spoken through the prophets (Luke 1:68–70). Paul likewise wrote to the Hebrews: “In many portions and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets; at the end of these days he has spoken to us in a Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). And to the Corinthians he wrote about the Son: “since you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me” (2 Corinthians 13:3). And the Savior himself teaches in Matthew: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father is the one who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).
That for the same reason, namely that the Trinity is of one essence, it is written that we live to the Father, to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

The fact that Scripture says we live to the Father, to the Son and to the Holy Spirit also teaches us to see this most plainly. So Paul argues in his letter to the Romans: “Count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11). And again: “that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for Christ, who died and was raised for them” (2 Corinthians 5:15). And to the Galatians: “If we live to the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25).
That for this reason it is written that the law from above belongs to the Father, to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

For the reason we have given, the law from above is also written to be the law of the Father, of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. So the sacred psalmist says in Psalm 37: “The law of his God is in his heart” (Psalm 37:31); and in Psalm 40: “I have willed to do your will, O God, and your law is in the midst of my inmost parts” (Psalm 40:8). So too Paul writes to the Galatians: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). And to the Corinthians, in the first letter: “To those without the law I became as one without the law, not being without the law of God but under the law of Christ, that I might win those without the law” (1 Corinthians 9:21). And to the Romans: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and of death” (Romans 8:2). And again, hinting at the new covenant and the old, he says: “But now we have been released from the law, having died to that in which we were held, so that we serve in newness of the Spirit and not in oldness of the letter” (Romans 7:6). And again: “For we know that the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14).
That for the same cause, the one essence of the Trinity, we are called men of God, or Christians, or spiritual.

This, then, is why we are called either men of God, or Christians, or spiritual. We hear these names from the widow in Zarephath, who says to Elijah the Tishbite: “What is there between me and you, man of God?” (1 Kings 17:18), and again: “Now I know that you are a holy man of God” (1 Kings 17:24). The Shunammite says to her husband about the prophet Elisha: “See, a great man of God is coming to us” (2 Kings 4:9). The histories of the Kings say: “And a man of God came out of Judah and prophesied against the altar in Bethel” (1 Kings 13:1–2). The sacred psalmist, in the heading of Psalm 90, says: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God” (Psalm 90). Paul, writing to Timothy for the second time, says: “that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:17). The Acts say: “It came about that for a whole year they were gathered together in the church, and that the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch” (Acts 11:26). And Paul, discoursing with the Corinthians in a letter, says: “Now about spiritual things, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were Gentiles you were carried off to the voiceless idols, however you happened to be led. Therefore …” (1 Corinthians 12:1–3).

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u07): retranslated from the Greek. The old draft printed edition numbers 21-24 and ran the four chapter titles into the text; made the Trinity the thing spoken 'of' instead of the speaker 'in' believers (21.ν); twice read λόγος (reason) as 'the Word' (22.ν, 23.1, where 'Because of whom we said it is the Word' was garbled); rendered κοιλία 'womb'. Wrong psalms: 'Psalm 40' for LXX 36 (English 37:31), 'Psalm 39:8' for LXX 39 (English 40:8), 'the 89th Psalm (Ps 89 LXX)' for the heading of English Psalm 90. Abbreviated references written out; chapter titles 21-24 set as their own paragraphs.
